info.name: ModaCo — Promotion Management API
info.description:
Manual test collection for the ModaCo Promotion Management API.

## Setup
```bash
npx prisma migrate deploy
npm run seed       # 6 products + 2 promotions showing precedence
npm run dev        # API on :3000
npm run worker     # required only for Scenario A
```

## Folders
- **Health** — liveness and dependency status
- **Products** — read paths, including the effective-price sort
- **Promotions** — create / cancel / assign
- **Scenario B — Flash Sale Walkthrough** — run in order; proves instant invalidation and clean reversal
- **Scenario A — Bulk Ingestion** — 500k-row import; self-polls to completion
- **Validation & Conflicts** — negative cases, each naming the layer that rejected it

## Notes
- `productId`, `promotionId` and `jobId` are captured automatically by test scripts — run **List products** first so `productId` is populated.
- Responses carry `X-Cache: l1 | l2 | miss | bypass`, so caching behaviour is observable per request.
- The **List products** tests include a numeric-monotonicity guard on `effectivePrice`. It exists because this endpoint once sorted lexicographically (`'100.00'` before `'30.00'`) while still returning a plausible-looking ordered list. See ADR-007.
- Several requests mutate state. The walkthrough and validation folders clean up after themselves; re-run `npm run seed` to reset.
- Every route sits behind a per-route-class rate limiter (`X-RateLimit-*` headers). Reads, `?at=` simulations, promotion writes and the ingestion trigger have separate budgets. The limiter **fails open** if Redis is unavailable, so a cache outage cannot become a storefront outage. The 429 path is asserted in `tests/hardening.test.ts` rather than here, because consuming a shared IP-keyed budget mid-collection would make the rest of the run flaky.

request.description: Guards against a single request sorting and serialising an unbounded slice of the catalogue.

Prices the catalogue at an arbitrary instant, so a scheduled flash sale can be verified before it goes live.

The instant is snapped to the minute and the result is cached. Simulations used to bypass the cache entirely — rare enough not to pollute it — but that made ?at=<unique> an unauthenticated, unbounded-cost request: ~380ms of database work each time, rationed only by the caller's patience. Snapping collapses the key space so repeats hit cache; minute granularity keeps a sale starting at 14:30 visible to someone probing 14:31.

request.description: Re-targets an existing promotion. The same EXCLUDE constraint guards this path, because the constraint is on the table's state rather than on the insert — which is the payoff for putting the rule in the schema instead of in a create-time service check.

item.name: Scenario A — Bulk Ingestion
item.description:
500,000-row vendor import under serverless constraints.

**Prerequisites**
1. `npm run generate:vendor-file -- 500000` — writes ~28 MB into ./storage
2. `npm run worker` — the chunk processor must be running

The trigger deliberately takes a blob-storage *key*, not an upload: pushing hundreds of megabytes through a request handler would hold the request open for the whole job, which is the exact failure mode the design avoids.

**Try killing the worker mid-run and restarting it** — the job resumes from its last completed chunk.

request.description: Returns 202 immediately. The endpoint writes one row and enqueues one message; all real work happens in short-lived worker invocations.

item.name: Start ingestion job — 404 unknown file key

request.description: Fails fast at the trigger so the caller learns immediately, rather than through a job that fails asynchronously. An unresolvable key is a caller mistake, so it is translated to 404 rather than surfacing a raw storage ENOENT as a 500.

Per-chunk state, rows processed, and rejected-row counts.

This request **re-runs itself** in the Collection Runner until the job reaches a terminal state (capped at 60 polls). Set a ~1000 ms delay in the Runner so polling is not tight-looped.

item.name: Validation & Conflicts
item.description:
Negative cases. Each one is rejected by a specific layer — schema validation, a CHECK constraint, or an EXCLUDE constraint — and the error code says which.

These are deterministic against `npm run seed`, which leaves an active 50% flash sale on `accessories`.

item.name: 409 — overlapping promotion on an already-promoted category

request.description: The core business rule: at most one active promotion per target at a time. Enforced by `promotions_no_overlap_per_category`.

item.name: 201 — adjacent window is NOT a conflict

request.description:
The window is half-open `[starts, ends)`, so a promotion ending exactly when the next begins is a clean handover rather than an overlap. This one sits entirely in the future and is accepted.

Cancel it afterwards via the captured `adjacentPromotionId`.

item.name: Clean up — cancel the adjacent promotion

request.description: Would invert the price. Caught by schema validation; also backed by the `promotions_value_chk` CHECK constraint, so a direct database write cannot bypass it either.

A CATEGORY-scope promotion must carry a `category`, never a `productId`. Without this rule a row could claim one scope while carrying the other's payload, and the resolution query would silently mis-attribute the discount. Mirrored by `promotions_scope_payload_chk` in the DDL.

item.name: 404 — promotion for a product that does not exist

request.description: Half of the original DoS vector. Sorting by effective price cannot use an index, so a deep OFFSET sorts every row before it. The bound is on the computed offset (page-1)*limit rather than on `page` alone, because page=1000&limit=100 is a hundred times more expensive than page=1000&limit=1.

item.name: 400 — the original attack request is now refused

exec: // The exact request that measured ~380ms of uncached database work per call.

request.description: `?at=<unique>&page=400000` combined an uncacheable read with an attacker-controlled OFFSET. Both halves are now bounded, and the request is rejected at the edge rather than reaching the database.

This route used to parse `at` with a bare new Date(String(...)), so a garbage value became an Invalid Date and was handed to the query layer. It is now validated by the same schema the list endpoint uses.
